Attainment and Attendance in Crawley

What the national model behind How to Pull the Right Lever says about the district’s secondary schools, within West Sussex and alongside Brighton and Hove. Draft for discussion.

Author
Affiliation

Adam Dennett

Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, University College London

Published

October 31, 2026

WarningDraft for discussion

One of the district documents for Sussex. It sits beneath the West Sussex document, and the district summary compares all of the districts. Every figure comes from published Department for Education data and the national models of How to Pull the Right Lever. Nothing uses pupil-level records. The commentary is written to a common pattern from the figures; read it as a starting point for discussion.

Summary

Crawley’s results are among the weakest of England’s districts, on an intake less disadvantaged than England’s. Its 7 state secondary schools are in Crawley.

  • Overall results: 42.1 in Attainment 8 in 2024/25, 235th of 264 districts in England.
  • Disadvantage: 23.4% of pupils are disadvantaged, against 28.3% nationally.
  • Disadvantaged pupils average 30.7, below the national 37.8 (255th of 264).
  • The gap between disadvantaged pupils and the rest is 14.6 points, the 69th widest of 264.

The other findings:

  • For all pupils, Crawley is 4.6 points below England. The largest pieces in the national model are prior attainment (-1.5) and West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-0.7). The district’s schools take 3.3 points beyond what the model expects.
  • For disadvantaged pupils it is 5.3 points below England. The largest pieces are West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-1.5) and being in the South East (-1.3), and the schools take 2.6 points beyond what the model expects.
  • Part of the district effect survives each school’s own record. For non-disadvantaged pupils (-3.5%) it remains with each school’s own record in the model: the nearest thing to a genuine place effect.
  • None of the 7 schools is above expectation over 2021/22 to 2024/25. The strongest is Holy Trinity CofE Secondary School, Crawley (-1.1); the weakest Thomas Bennett Community College (-6.0).
  • Absence was 8.3% in autumn and spring 2025/26 (8.8% a year earlier), against 8.0% for England and 8.1% for West Sussex. Over 2021/22 to 2024/25 its schools ran in line with what their intakes predict, and Holy Trinity CofE Secondary School, Crawley and Thomas Bennett Community College more than a point above.
  • Reduced timetables run at 2.1 times the national rate, and suspensions at 0.9 times (18.5 per 100 pupils, against 21.2).
  • Disadvantaged groups are small, 26 to 67 pupils a year per school. Every school-level figure for them moves from year to year and should be read over several years.

1 About this analysis

Crawley is a district of West Sussex, not a local authority, and that shapes what can be said:

  • The national models place schools in local authorities. The “local authority effect” in this document is West Sussex’s, shared with every school in the county.
  • What is particular to Crawley shows up in its schools’ own residuals, and in the district test of Section 6.
  • Absence and exclusions are summed over the district’s 7 schools, followed through any change of URN.

The methods are described in full in the East Sussex document.

4 What explains attainment in Crawley

The decomposition for Crawley, in Attainment 8 points. ‘Place’ is West Sussex’s effect plus the South East’s; ‘unexplained’ is what the district’s own schools add beyond everything the model accounts for.

For all pupils, Crawley is 4.6 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • prior attainment (-1.51);
  • West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-0.74);
  • being in the South East (-0.46);
  • English as an additional language (+0.29);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (-3.25), beyond what the model expects.

For disadvantaged pupils, Crawley is 5.3 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-1.47);
  • being in the South East (-1.32);
  • prior attainment (-1.00);
  • English as an additional language (+0.80);
  • admissions (-0.30);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (-2.61), beyond what the model expects.

6 Is there a Crawley effect?

The district test of the East Sussex document adds a district level to the national model, with and without each school’s own record.

On the published model, Crawley differs from the rest of West Sussex for all pupils (-5.2%), disadvantaged pupils (-5.1%) and non-disadvantaged pupils (-5.8%). With each school’s own record in the model, the effect for non-disadvantaged pupils (-3.5%) remains. That is the nearest thing in the data to a genuine place effect: something all the district’s schools share.

7 Absence

  • 8.3% absence in autumn and spring 2025/26, against 8.0% for England and 8.1% for West Sussex. A year earlier it was 8.8%.
  • Persistent absence is 22.7%, against 21.6% for England.
  • Against its intake, the district’s schools run 0.01 points above what their pupils’ profiles predict, on average over 2021/22 to 2024/25.
  • Holy Trinity CofE Secondary School, Crawley and Thomas Bennett Community College each run more than a point above their predicted absence.
  • Hazelwick School runs more than a point below its prediction.

Reduced timetables account for 0.60% of sessions, against 0.29% in England, 2.1 times the national rate. Holy Trinity CofE Secondary School, Crawley’s rate is the highest in the district.

5 of the 7 schools are above the national average absence in 2024/25. Bringing them to it would add up to 3.0 points for all pupils, as an indication of scale.

Suspensions were 18.5 per 100 pupils in 2024/25, against 21.2 for England and 16.2 for West Sussex.

9 Questions for discussion

  1. Disadvantaged pupils. They average 30.7 in Crawley against 37.8 in England, and the district’s schools take 2.6 points for them beyond what the model expects. What does Ifield Community College, above expectation for these pupils, do that the district’s other schools could share?
  2. Attendance is not the district’s main lever. Absence makes almost no difference to its results against England, though Holy Trinity CofE Secondary School, Crawley and Thomas Bennett Community College run more absence than their intakes predict.
  3. Something the district’s schools share. The effect for non-disadvantaged pupils (-3.5%) survives each school’s own record. What do all Crawley schools have in common that its neighbours do not?
  4. Practice. In Crawley, reduced timetables run at 2.1 times the national rate. These are choices made within schools, and neighbouring districts make them differently.
  5. The county. West Sussex’s own effect for disadvantaged pupils is -3.8% (131st of 151), distinguishable from zero, and it applies to every school here. The county questions in the West Sussex document apply here as well.

Notes on method

Methods and sources are those of the East Sussex document. District membership comes from each school’s postcode (ONS postcode directory, via postcodes.io). Absence and exclusions for the district are summed over its schools, including any predecessor or successor URNs. This document is generated from templates/district_report.qmd by R/20_district_reports.R, from data built by R/17_area_analysis.R, R/18_district_effects.R and R/19_trust_effects.R. Its format is described in AREA_REPORTS.md.
